en.title: Nuclear risk
en.summary: Nuclear risk refers to the danger that nuclear weapons will be used, whether deliberately or accidentally, causing mass human casualties through both direct blast damage and effects on the climate. While direct deaths from blast and heat could reach the millions, the "nuclear winter" caused by soot reaching the stratosphere is projected to collapse agriculture and expand the toll to billions. The number of nuclear warheads has fallen sharply since the end of the Cold War, yet more than 10,000 nuclear weapons remain across nine countries — enough, even at that scale, to trigger unprecedented climate change.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## Damage in two stages

Measuring the danger of [nuclear weapons](/hubpedia/nuclear-weapon) by the destructive power of a single detonation alone misjudges the scale of the harm. If one nuclear weapon were detonated over a city, the shock wave and heat could take millions of lives almost immediately. Alongside that, however, there is a pathway through which billions could die by way of effects on agriculture. Nuclear risk is the umbrella term for the danger of nuclear weapons being used, encompassing both stages — the direct and the indirect damage. [1][37]

The direct damage does not end at the moment of detonation. Radioactive fallout produced by the explosion is lofted into the atmosphere, spreads across large parts of the world, and settles to the ground, delivering lethal radiation doses. Cities that are attacked burn so intensely that they generate their own wind systems, producing what is known as a "firestorm." [2][8]

## Nuclear winter and nuclear famine

The columns of smoke and soot rising from these firestorms reach as high as the stratosphere. According to estimates by the researcher Robock, smoke and soot would reach an altitude of 40 kilometers (25 miles). Soot that reaches the stratosphere is not washed out by rain, so it lingers for years, darkening the sky and drying and cooling the planet. [9][10][47]

This cooling is the phenomenon known as "nuclear winter." After a large-scale nuclear war, temperature drops of 20 to 30 degrees are projected across many of the world's agricultural regions, including Eurasia and North America. The main mechanism by which food production declines is the shortening of the growing season — that is, the number of consecutive frost-free days. In addition, this scenario is expected to destroy the ozone layer, allowing more ultraviolet radiation to reach the surface and harm plants and animals. [3][43][48]

The result is "nuclear famine," in which global [food production](/hubpedia/food-supply) collapses and billions are projected to starve to death. Before dying of hunger, though, many people are expected to die of hypothermia. [4][61]

Recognition of this risk is relatively recent. The danger of nuclear winter (initially called "nuclear twilight") was discovered in the early 1980s, more than 30 years after nuclear weapons were first used. In other words, nuclear weapons were built and deployed for decades without their most far-reaching consequences being understood. [36]

## The nuclear-armed states and the size of their stockpiles

Nine countries are known to possess nuclear weapons: Russia, the United States, France, China, the United Kingdom, Israel, Pakistan, India, and North Korea. More than 10,000 nuclear weapons exist today, distributed across at least these nine countries, and the world's nuclear powers hold more than 12,000 warheads in total. [5][6][14]

Stockpile sizes differ greatly from country to country. Many hold tens to hundreds of weapons, while Russia and the United States hold thousands. A substantial share of warheads is deployed on ballistic missiles or at bomber bases, ready for rapid use. In terms of purpose, they divide into strategic weapons aimed at targets far from the battlefield, such as military industry and infrastructure, and non-strategic or tactical weapons intended for use on the battlefield. [38][50][62]

## Yield and destructive power over time

The atomic bomb the United States dropped on Hiroshima in August 1945 had a yield of 13 to 18 kilotons of TNT equivalent. Many of the nuclear weapons that exist today are far larger than those dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The United States rapidly developed far more powerful warheads during the 1950s, and the Soviet Union increased its destructive power more gradually, eventually reaching a comparable level. The largest nuclear explosion in history was the "Tsar Bomba," built by the Soviet Union and detonated in October 1961, with a yield of about 50 megatons (50,000 kilotons) — roughly 3,333 times that of the Hiroshima bomb. [7][13][20][33][54]

Total stockpiles grew for nearly half a century after their emergence in the 1940s, peaking above 60,000 weapons in 1986. The destructive power of first-strike warheads peaked in the early 1980s at more than 15,000 megatons, a yield equivalent to more than a million Hiroshima bombs. At that time, first-strike nuclear weapons had the capacity to destroy more than 40% of the world's urban land. [17][21][45][55][56]

Since the end of the Cold War, global nuclear stockpiles have been reduced substantially. The number of warheads fell below 20,000 in the 2010s, but total stockpiles still exceed 10,000. Even now, the destructive power of first-strike warheads exceeds 2,500 megatons and could directly destroy about 7% of the world's urban land. Some countries are expanding their nuclear arsenals. [18][19][39][53][57]

The scale of the reductions is large, but that does not mean the danger has disappeared. Research by Robock, Oman, and Stenchikov (2007) showed that even assuming stockpiles after the deep post-Cold War reductions, enough weapons remain in the world to cause "large, long-lasting, unprecedented climate change." Even a war fought with today's reduced stockpiles alone is assumed to kill billions under nuclear winter scenarios. [34][49][60]

## Uses and near-uses

Nuclear weapons have been used in war only once, against Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing between 110,000 and 210,000 people. Since then, the world has come close to using them again more than a dozen times. These cases include both accidental and deliberate ones. [15][27][44][58][64]

The pathways to use are not limited to deliberate attacks between states. Risk factors also include the possibility that nuclear terrorist groups seize a weapon, that hackers take over nuclear command systems, and that a deeply irresponsible leader heads a nuclear-armed state. Several countries keep their nuclear weapons on "launch on warning" alert, in which leaders receiving a warning can decide within minutes to launch a retaliatory strike. Taking nuclear weapons off this posture is said to reduce the risk that an accident, once it occurs, spirals rapidly out of control. [35][41][46][59]

## Nuclear testing over time and its effects

The nuclear-armed states once tested frequently. The number of tests peaked at 178 in 1962, most of them conducted by the United States and the Soviet Union. These tests harmed the environment and people, especially Indigenous communities. [22][23][24]

Testing declined in the later Cold War and has been rare over the past two decades. The only country to have conducted nuclear tests in recent years is North Korea. [25][26]

## Curbing proliferation, and treaties

The number of countries seeking nuclear weapons did not grow as much as was once expected. In the late 1970s, more than a dozen countries were considering or pursuing nuclear weapons, but most of them stopped. In recent years, only Syria has considered acquiring them, and only Iran has actually pursued development. South Africa once possessed nuclear weapons and became the first country to give them up voluntarily. [12][16][51][52]

The treaty framework is divided by purpose. Most countries have approved the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, which aim to end nuclear testing. The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons has also been approved by many countries, with the purpose of preventing the spread of nuclear weapons. In recent years, dozens of countries have approved the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which aims to end the development and the very existence of nuclear weapons and entered into force in 2021. Meanwhile, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty between the United States and Russia has lapsed. [11][28][29][30][42]

## The difficulty of assessment

Nuclear war would inflict catastrophic damage on every country, including the one that launched the attack. U.S. President Reagan said that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought." [31][32]

There is no settled view on the upper bound of the damage. Researchers disagree about how likely it is that nuclear winter would kill off humanity entirely, and it is unclear whether the human species could survive an all-out nuclear war at current stockpile levels. What can be said with certainty is that nuclear weapons capable of killing billions continue to exist in the world, and uncertainty about whether that would amount to extinction of the species does not weaken the assessment that harm on that scale could occur. [40][60][63]

title: 犯罪率
summary: 犯罪率は、一定期間に発生した犯罪の件数を人口規模で割った指標で、通常は人口10万人あたりの件数で示される。米国では暴力犯罪率・財産犯罪率のいずれも1990年代前半のピーク以降に大きく低下した一方、世論調査では多くの回答者が前年より犯罪が増えたと答え続けてきた。数値は実際の発生状況だけでなく、犯罪の定義や集計方式の変更によっても動く。
bodyMarkdown:
## 暴力犯罪と財産犯罪の区分

犯罪率は犯罪をまとめて数えた指標ではなく、どの行為をどの分類に入れるかを決めた上で集計される。米国の統計における暴力犯罪には、殺人（謀殺および故殺）、レイプ、強盗、加重暴行が含まれる。このうち殺人は、個人的な理由により意図的かつ違法に他者を殺害することであり、最も重大な犯罪と位置づけられる。 [9][31]

財産犯罪には、住居侵入盗、窃盗（住居侵入を伴わない軽微な盗み）、盗品犯罪、放火などが含まれる。ただし放火の扱いは他の類型と同じではない。FBIによれば、放火については傾向表や検挙率表にデータが含まれているものの、総数を推計するのに十分なデータがない。 [11][20]

## 暴力犯罪率の長期推移

米国の暴力犯罪率は1980年代に上昇し、1990年代前半に人口10万人あたり約750件でピークに達した。その後は長期の低下が続き、ピーク時以降、暴力犯罪率は半分以下に減少した。 [1][7]

低下の幅は犯罪の種類によって異なる。殺人率はほぼ半減し、加重暴行は40%減少した一方、強盗は約80%減少しており、総体としての減少は特定の類型に強く引かれている。 [2]

低下は一本調子ではなかった。殺人と暴行の発生率は2020年と2021年に増加したが、その後再び減少した。 [8]

## 財産犯罪率の長期推移

財産犯罪率も1980年代から1990年代前半にかけて高く、ピーク時には人口10万人あたり約5,000件だった。その水準は過去30年間で60%減少し、財産犯罪の被害率はピーク以降50人に1人未満にまで低下した。 [12][13][27]

内訳の動き方は一様ではない。窃盗（larceny）と住居侵入盗（burglary）は1990年代以降、着実な減少傾向をたどってきた。これに対して自動車盗難は変動が大きく、1990年代前後により顕著なピークを迎え、2000年代初頭に増加へ転じ、直近5年間でもわずかに増加している。 [28][29]

実数で見ると、1991年には米国で約170万台の自動車が盗まれた。近年、米国の盗難自動車の件数は70万台から100万台の間で推移している。 [6][14]

## 集計方式の変更と数値への影響

集計の規則そのものが件数を左右する。FBIのSummary Reporting Systemのデータセットでは、同一事件で複数の犯罪が発生した場合、最も重い犯罪のみが記録される。より詳細な記録方式であるNIBRSへの移行により、全国の犯罪率は全体で約2%増加した。この増加は事件の実数が増えたことではなく、記録の仕方が変わったことによる。 [18][32]

変化の大きさは類型ごとに異なり、NIBRSへの移行はレイプで0.1%未満、強盗と加重暴行で0.6%、住居侵入盗で1.0%、窃盗で2.6%、自動車盗難で2.7%の増加をもたらした。数値としては小さいが、移行の前後をまたいで長期の推移を読む場合には、実際の変化と記録方法の変化を分けて考える必要がある。 [19]

## レイプの定義変更（2013年）

FBIは2013年に統一犯罪報告プログラムにおけるレイプの定義を変更した。旧来のレイプの定義は「女性に対する強制的かつ本人の意思に反した性交」とされており、男性被害者を含まず、他の性的暴行犯罪も含んでいなかった。この定義変更は、パート1犯罪について80年の歴史の中で初めての変更だった。 [3][10][21][22]

改定されたレイプの定義には男性および非バイナリーの被害者が含まれる。また、本人の同意のない口腔・肛門性交や物を用いた性的暴行など、他の性的暴行犯罪も含まれる。 [23][24]

変更の効果は、同じ年のデータを新旧両方の定義で集計すると明確になる。2013年のFBIデータでは、強制性交と定義される女性被害者のレイプ件数は旧定義・新定義ともに26,994件で同じだった。改定定義では、男性被害者のレイプ611件、同意のない口腔・肛門性交（「ソドミー」に分類）7,602件、物を用いた性的暴行3,043件が追加で計上された。つまり増加分は、それまで数えられていなかった行為と被害者が新たに集計に入ったことによる。 [4][5]

そのため推移も定義ごとに分けて読む必要がある。女性に対するレイプ（狭い旧定義）は1990年代前半のピークから2010年代前半にかけて減少し、その後、レイプ率はわずかに上昇し始めた。改定定義でのレイプ率は2020年まで増加した後、2010年代半ばと同水準まで低下した。 [25][26][34]

## 世界の殺人率

低下は米国に限られた現象ではなく、世界全体で見ても、殺人率は近年数十年で低下している。ただし水準は国によって大きく異なり、殺人は世界的に一般的な死亡原因であり、一部の国では主要なものとなっている。 [30][33]

## 統計上の推移と一般の認識の差

統計上の減少幅は大きい。1990年代の米国人は、今日と比べて少なくとも2倍犯罪の被害に遭いやすかった。それでも[人々の認識](/hubpedia/perception-of-progress)は同じ方向を向いていない。ギャラップ社の年次調査27回のうち23回で、多数派の回答者が前年より犯罪率が増加したと信じていた。 [15][16]

報道での扱われ方と実際の頻度の隔たりも測定されている。殺人は[死因](/hubpedia/cause-of-death)を扱う報道の40%から50%を占める一方、実際の死亡者数に占める割合は1%未満だった。 [17]

en.title: Crime rate
en.summary: The crime rate is a measure of the number of crimes committed over a given period divided by the size of the population, usually expressed as offenses per 100,000 people. In the United States, both the violent crime rate and the property crime rate have fallen sharply since their peak in the early 1990s, yet in opinion polls a majority of respondents have continued to say that crime rose compared with the previous year. The figures move not only with actual conditions but also with changes in how crimes are defined and tabulated.
en.bodyMarkdown:
## The division between violent crime and property crime

The crime rate is not a measure that counts crimes in the aggregate; it is compiled after deciding which acts fall into which category. Violent crime in U.S. statistics includes homicide (murder and manslaughter), rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. Of these, homicide — the intentional and unlawful killing of another person for personal reasons — is treated as the most serious offense. [9][31]

Property crime includes burglary, larceny (minor theft not involving unlawful entry), offenses involving stolen property, and arson. Arson, however, is not handled in the same way as the other categories. According to the FBI, data on arson is included in trend and clearance tables, but there is not sufficient data to estimate totals. [11][20]

## The long-term trend in the violent crime rate

The violent crime rate in the United States rose during the 1980s and peaked in the early 1990s at roughly 750 offenses per 100,000 people. A long decline followed, and since that peak the violent crime rate has fallen by more than half. [1][7]

The size of the decline varies by type of crime. The homicide rate fell by nearly half and aggravated assault fell by 40%, while robbery fell by about 80%, so the overall decrease is pulled strongly by particular categories. [2]

The decline was not uninterrupted. Rates of homicide and assault increased in 2020 and 2021 before falling again. [8]

## The long-term trend in the property crime rate

The property crime rate was also high from the 1980s into the early 1990s, reaching roughly 5,000 offenses per 100,000 people at its peak. That level has fallen by 60% over the past 30 years, and the victimization rate for property crime has dropped to fewer than 1 in 50 people since the peak. [12][13][27]

The components have not moved uniformly. Larceny and burglary have followed a steady downward trend since the 1990s. Motor vehicle theft, by contrast, has fluctuated more, with a more pronounced peak around the 1990s, a turn back upward in the early 2000s, and a slight increase over the past five years as well. [28][29]

In absolute numbers, about 1.7 million vehicles were stolen in the United States in 1991. In recent years, the number of stolen vehicles in the United States has ranged between 700,000 and 1 million. [6][14]

## Changes in tabulation methods and their effect on the figures

The recording rules themselves affect the counts. In the FBI's Summary Reporting System dataset, when multiple crimes occur in a single incident, only the most serious offense is recorded. The move to NIBRS, a more detailed recording method, raised the national crime rate by roughly 2% overall. That increase reflects a change in how incidents are recorded, not an increase in the actual number of incidents. [18][32]

The magnitude of the change differs by category: the transition to NIBRS produced increases of less than 0.1% for rape, 0.6% for robbery and aggravated assault, 1.0% for burglary, 2.6% for larceny, and 2.7% for motor vehicle theft. The figures are small, but when reading long-term trends that span the transition, actual change has to be separated from change in recording method. [19]

## The 2013 change to the definition of rape

In 2013 the FBI changed the definition of rape used in the Uniform Crime Reporting Program. The former definition of rape was "the carnal knowledge of a female forcibly and against her will," which excluded male victims and did not cover other sexual assault offenses. This was the first change to a Part 1 offense in the program's 80-year history. [3][10][21][22]

The revised definition of rape includes male and non-binary victims. It also includes other sexual assault offenses, such as non-consensual oral or anal sex and sexual assault with an object. [23][24]

The effect of the change becomes clear when the same year's data is tabulated under both the old and the new definition. In the FBI's 2013 data, the number of rapes of female victims defined as forcible intercourse was 26,994 under both the old and the new definition. The revised definition added 611 rapes of male victims, 7,602 instances of non-consensual oral or anal sex (classified as "sodomy"), and 3,043 sexual assaults with an object. The increase, in other words, came from acts and victims that had not previously been counted entering the tally. [4][5]

For that reason the trend must also be read separately by definition. Rape of women (the narrow, older definition) declined from its early-1990s peak into the early 2010s, after which the rape rate began to rise slightly. Under the revised definition, the rape rate increased through 2020 and then fell back to about the level of the mid-2010s. [25][26][34]

## Homicide rates worldwide

The decline is not confined to the United States; worldwide as well, homicide rates have fallen in recent decades. Levels differ widely by country, however, and homicide is a common cause of death globally, and a leading one in some countries. [30][33]

## The gap between the statistical trend and public perception

The statistical decline is large. Americans in the 1990s were at least twice as likely to be victims of crime as they are today. Even so, [public perception](/hubpedia/perception-of-progress) does not point the same way. In 23 of 27 annual Gallup surveys, a majority of respondents believed the crime rate had increased over the previous year. [15][16]

The gap between how crime is covered and how often it actually occurs has also been measured. Homicide accounted for 40% to 50% of news coverage of [causes of death](/hubpedia/cause-of-death), while making up less than 1% of actual deaths. [17]

claims.statement: ピーク時以降、暴力犯罪率は半分以下に減少した。

evidence.quote: Since then, rates have more than halved.

claims.statement: 殺人と暴行の発生率は2020年と2021年に増加したが、その後再び減少した。

evidence.quote: Homicide and assault rates increased in 2020 and 2021, but have since fallen again.

claims.statement: 米国の統計における暴力犯罪には、殺人（謀殺および故殺）、レイプ、強盗、加重暴行が含まれる。

evidence.quote: In US statistics, this includes homicide (murder and non-negligent manslaughter), rape, robbery, and aggravated assault.

claims.statement: 旧来のレイプの定義は「女性に対する強制的かつ本人の意思に反した性交」とされていた。

evidence.quote: carnal knowledge of a female forcibly and against her will

claims.statement: 財産犯罪には、住居侵入盗、窃盗（住居侵入を伴わない軽微な盗み）、盗品犯罪、放火などが含まれる。

evidence.quote: Property crimes involve the stealing, damage, or destruction of someone’s property. This includes offenses such as burglary, larceny (which is more like pickpocketing, and without breaking and entering), theft, and arson.

claims.statement: 財産犯罪率は1980年代から1990年代前半にかけて高かったが、過去30年間で60%減少した。

evidence.quote: Rates were high throughout the 1980s and into the early 1990s, but have fallen by 60% in the last 30 years.

claims.statement: 財産犯罪率はピーク時に人口10万人あたり約5,000件だった。

evidence.quote: At the peak, there were around 5,000 offenses per 100,000 people.

claims.statement: 近年、米国の盗難自動車の件数は70万台から100万台の間で推移している。

evidence.quote: In recent years, that number has fluctuated between 700,000 and 1 million.

claims.statement: 1990年代の米国人は、今日と比べて少なくとも2倍犯罪の被害に遭いやすかった。

evidence.quote: Americans in the 1990s were at least twice as likely to be victims of crime as they are today.

claims.statement: ギャラップ社の年次調査27回のうち23回で、多数派の回答者が前年より犯罪率が増加したと信じていた。

evidence.quote: In 23 out of the 27 annual surveys, the majority said that they believed crime rates had increased from the previous year.

claims.statement: 殺人は「死因」報道の40%から50%を占める一方、実際の死亡者数に占める割合は1%未満だった。

evidence.quote: Homicides received 40% to 50% of “causes of death” coverage, despite making up less than 1% of deaths.

claims.statement: NIBRSへの移行により、全国の犯罪率は全体で約2%増加した。

evidence.quote: Overall, the transition to the NIBRS increased national crime rates by around 2%.

claims.statement: NIBRSへの移行は、レイプで0.1%未満、強盗と加重暴行で0.6%、住居侵入盗で1.0%、窃盗で2.6%、自動車盗難で2.7%の増加をもたらした。

evidence.quote: less than a 0.1% increase for rape, a 0.6% increase for robbery and aggravated assault, a 1.0% increase for burglary, a 2.6% increase for larceny, and a 2.7% increase for motor vehicle theft.

claims.statement: FBIによれば、放火については傾向表・検挙率表にデータが含まれているものの、総数を推計するのに十分なデータがない。

evidence.quote: Although arson data are included in the trend and clearance tables, sufficient data are not available to estimate totals for this offense.

claims.statement: この定義変更は、パート1犯罪について80年の歴史の中で初めての変更だった。

evidence.quote: This was the first time it had done so in its 80-year history for a Part 1 offense.

claims.statement: 旧定義は男性被害者を含まず、他の性的暴行犯罪も含んでいなかった。

evidence.quote: It did not include male victims, nor did it include other sexual assault offenses.

claims.statement: 改定されたレイプの定義には男性および非バイナリーの被害者が含まれる。

evidence.quote: it includes male and non-binary victims

claims.statement: 改定された定義には、本人の同意のない口腔・肛門性交や物を用いた性的暴行など、他の性的暴行犯罪も含まれる。

evidence.quote: it includes other sexual assault crimes, including oral and anal sex against someone’s consent, and sexual assault with an object.

claims.statement: 女性に対するレイプ（狭い旧定義）は1990年代前半のピークから2010年代前半にかけて減少した。

evidence.quote: rape of women (using the narrower definition) became less common from a peak in the early 1990s, through to the early 2010s.

claims.statement: 改定定義でのレイプ率は2020年まで増加した後、2010年代半ばと同水準まで低下した。

evidence.quote: The revised definition shows an increase to 2020, before falling back to rates equivalent to the mid-2010s.

claims.statement: 財産犯罪の被害率は、ピーク以降50人に1人未満にまで低下した。

evidence.quote: Since then, it has fallen to fewer than 1 per 50 people.

claims.statement: 窃盗（larceny）と住居侵入盗（burglary）は1990年代以降、着実な減少傾向をたどってきた。

evidence.quote: Larceny and burglary have mirrored the steady decline since the 1990s.

claims.statement: 自動車盗難は、1990年代前後により顕著なピークを迎え、2000年代初頭に増加へ転じ、直近5年間ではわずかに増加するなど、変動の大きい推移をたどってきた。

evidence.quote: Motor vehicle theft has been on a bumpier road, with a more distinct peak around the 1990s, a rebound in the early 2000s, and a smaller uptick in rates over the last five years.

claims.statement: 世界全体で見ても、殺人率は近年数十年で低下している。

evidence.quote: global homicide rates have gone down in recent decades.

claims.statement: 殺人とは、個人的な理由により意図的かつ違法に他者を殺害することであり、最も重大な犯罪である。

evidence.quote: Homicides — when people intentionally and illegally kill others for personal reasons — are the most serious crime.

claims.statement: FBIのSummary Reporting Systemのデータセットでは、同一事件で複数の犯罪が発生した場合、最も重い犯罪のみが記録される。

evidence.quote: if multiple crimes are committed in the same offense, the FBI only records the most serious crime in the dataset

claims.statement: 殺人は世界的に一般的な死因であり、一部の国では主要な死因となっている。

evidence.quote: They are a common cause of death globally and a leading cause of death in some countries.

claims.statement: その後、レイプ率はわずかに上昇し始めた。

evidence.quote: After that point, rates start to climb slightly.
